topComments.author: femto
topComments.text: What Woz did was the default way of writing assembly language programs for owners of 8-bit computers (mostly hobbyists). You didn't have money for a second machine, so you wrote your program on paper, you entered it then tested it in situ. Mostly you got it right, as doing it on paper was slow and meant you had the opportunity to put lots of thought into it. 8-bit instruction sets were simple enough that you eventually learned the most common instructions by heart. There was a point where I could mostly translate a Z80 program from assembly to machine code from (my) memory. Maybe that is part of the nostalgia for the 8-bit days: the practice of "slow programming"? It was relaxing, sort of like those "slow tv" shows.

topComments.author: david-gpu
topComments.text: I only had to assemble instructions by hand three times in my career. It is not difficult if you are already familiar with the ISA of that particular processor, but it is tedious. The first time was in my first job writing OpenGL ES 2.0 blending operations for the Imagination Technologies SGX 535, which was a remarkably advanced little GPU for its time. Alpha blending happened through special instructions in the fragment/pixel shader. We did have a compiler, but it didn't handle blending, for whatever reason. Through testing I noticed that NVidia GPUs performed blending incorrectly, according to the specification, which was a big surprise. Only years later I figured out that the specification had some errors; I now would bet that NVidia was doing the correct thing. The second time I had to assemble instructions by hand happened while working on a stripped down version of the Radeon 7xxx series that shipped on some mobile phones. I don't recall what the problem was, whether we were adding a feature or optimizing the microcode generated for a particular OpenGL operation, but it involved a rarely-used feature called user-defined clipping planes. We didn't have an assembler for that GPU; all microcode was assembled by hand. The third time happened at NVidia, and I will be vague, as not enough time has passed for me to be comfortable going into any detail. I had an idea for how to provide hardware acceleration for persistent CUDA kernels, which eventually was marketed as Cluster Launch Control (CLC). In order to quantify the benefit of adding some hardware, when it was possible to approximate that functionality in software, I needed to test the most efficient software implementation that was possible, and the compiler wasn't quite giving the assembly I wanted, so I had to manually patch some instructions post-compilation. Why did I not use the assembler that was available? I couldn't, because the assembly language did not provide a way to express the exact feature I had to patch.

stories.title: Understanding Positional Embeddings in Modern LLMs
stories.author: vismit2000

topComments.author: programjames
topComments.text: This article is only about understanding the implementation of positional embeddings, but to really understand positional embeddings you have to understand the theory. Positional embeddings are group representations. This is how you find them, and this is also how you parameterize them to make them differentiable/learnable. To give a few examples: 1. Rotary positional embeddings are representations of the translation group. The n-dimensional translation group ℝⁿ is abelian, so its irreducible representations are all one-dimensional ρ: ℝⁿ → ℂ, specified by a momentum vector m: ρₘ(x) = exp(i⟨m, x⟩). You can get a multi-dimensional representation by choosing several m, which are your learnable parameters. 2. If you wanted RoPE embeddings to also preserve rotation (perhaps you have scenes viewed at arbitrary angles), you are looking for representations of the special Euclidean group. The irreducible representations in four dimensions are your familiar particles: electrons, protons, etc., and in general are parameterized by a momentum vector and a discrete spin vector. You would have to do some kind of annealing process to train the spin vector (or you could just make it constant). 3. If you want to do attention on quadtrees, well, what is the group? Suppose every node in the quadtree has local coordinates scaled to [0, 1]. Moving up/down/to a neighbor in the quadtree requires an affine transformation of the local coordinates, which compose, so we can label every node by its affine transformation to the root (x, d): y → x + 2⁻ᵈy, where x is the node's translation in the image and d is its depth in the tree. The finite-dimensional irreducible representations are parameterized by momentum vectors m as well as a modulus M and basis vectors {e₁, e₂, ..., eₖ} where k = ord₂(M) and look like ρₘ,ₑ(x, d) = DPᵈ where D is the diagonal matrix with entries Dⱼⱼ = exp(2πi⟨2ʲm, x⟩ / M) and P permutes the basis vectors.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: IEEE 754 a bug?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: When working with floating-point arithmetic in almost any programming language, we encounter well-known precision issues, such as: 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 I am trying to understand how computer science classifies this behavior compared to historical time-related bugs like Y2K or the Year 2038 problem (Y2038). While Y2038 is widely considered a critical bug caused by storing time in a signed 32-bit integer, the 0.1 + 0.2 behavior stems from the IEEE 754 standard's inability to represent certain base-10 fractions accurately in base-2 (binary). From a software engineering and architectural perspective: 1. Why is IEEE 754 precision loss treated as an acceptable trade-off/feature rather than a massive bug, even though it has caused severe real-world failures (e.g., the Patriot missile failure)? 2. Are there fundamental differences in how standards bodies distinguish between a "hardware/math limitation" (IEEE 754) and an "overflow bug" (Y2038)?
